ukmt-cayley-2024-c1.title: Angles in isosceles triangles
ukmt-cayley-2024-c1.body:
Since $\angle B=90^\circ$, we have $\angle C=(90-a)^\circ$.

Because $AX=AB$, triangle $ABX$ is isosceles with apex $A$, so
$$\angle ABX=\frac{180^\circ-a^\circ}{2}=\left(90-\frac a2\right)^\circ .$$
Because $CY=CB$, triangle $CBY$ is isosceles with apex $C$, so
$$\angle CBY=\frac{180^\circ-(90-a)^\circ}{2}=\left(45+\frac a2\right)^\circ .$$

Since $AX+CY=AB+BC>AC$, the points lie in the order $A,Y,X,C$ on $AC$, so from $B$ the rays are in the order $BA,BY,BX,BC$. Hence
$$\angle ABX+\angle YBC=\angle ABC+\angle YBX,$$
because the angle $\angle YBX$ is counted twice on the left and $\angle ABC$ is the whole angle. Therefore
$$\angle XBY=\left(90-\frac a2\right)+\left(45+\frac a2\right)-90=45^\circ .$$
The value $a$ cancels, so $\angle XBY=45^\circ$ whatever the triangle.

**Answer: $45^\circ$** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2024-c2.title: Bound the number of correct answers, then give examples
ukmt-cayley-2024-c2.body:
Let Fiona answer $k$ questions correctly.

**$k\le 13$ is impossible.** Each correct answer is worth at most $6$, so she scores at most $13\times 6=78<80$.

**$k\ge 18$ is impossible.** At most $15$ of her correct answers are worth $5$, so at least $k-15$ are worth $6$ and her correct answers give at least $15\cdot 5+6(k-15)=6k-15$ marks. She has $25-k\le 7$ incorrect or blank answers, and the most these can cost is $5\times 2+2\times 1=12$ marks (five $-2$'s and two $-1$'s). So she scores at least $6k-15-12=6k-27\ge 6\cdot 18-27=81>80$.

**$k=14,15,16,17$ all occur:**
- $k=14$: correct on Questions 12-25 gives $4\times5+10\times6=80$.
- $k=15$: correct on Questions 6-20 gives $10\times5+5\times6=80$.
- $k=16$: correct on Questions 1-16 gives $75+6=81$; an incorrect answer to Question 17 costs $1$, total $80$.
- $k=17$: correct on Questions 1-17 gives $75+12=87$; incorrect answers to Questions 20, 21, 22, 23 cost $1+2+2+2=7$, total $80$.

**Answer: 14, 15, 16 or 17** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2024-c3.title: Repeated divisibility
ukmt-cayley-2024-c3.body:
Let $s$ be the digit sum of $N$. Since $39\mid N$, we have $3\mid N$, so $3\mid s$ (a number and its digit sum have the same remainder on division by $3$). So $s\ge3$ and $39\cdot3=117\mid N$.

Now $9\mid 117$, so $9\mid N$, hence $9\mid s$ and $39\cdot 9=351\mid N$.

The multiples of $351$ below $2024$ are $351,\ 702,\ 1053,\ 1404,\ 1755$.

- $351,702,1053,1404$ all have digit sum $9$, and each is a multiple of $39\times9=351$. They work.
- $1755$ has digit sum $18$, and $39\times 18=702$ does not divide $1755$ (it is odd). It fails.

**Answer: $N=351,\ 702,\ 1053,\ 1404$** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2024-c4.title: Use the median
ukmt-cayley-2024-c4.body:
The nine angles are $m-4d,\dots,m+4d$ in degrees, where $m$ is the middle one and $d>0$ (if $d=0$ every angle would be $60^\circ$). Their sum is $3\times180=540$, so $9m=540$ and $m=60$.

Since $42<60$, the angle $42^\circ$ is one of $m-4d,\ m-3d,\ m-2d,\ m-d$.

- $60-4d=42$: $d=4.5$. Angles $42,46.5,51,55.5,60,64.5,69,73.5,78$. They split into triangles $(42,64.5,73.5)$, $(46.5,55.5,78)$, $(51,60,69)$, each with sum $180$. Largest angle $78^\circ$.
- $60-3d=42$: $d=6$. Angles $36,42,48,54,60,66,72,78,84$, forming triangles $(36,66,78)$, $(42,54,84)$, $(48,60,72)$. Largest angle $84^\circ$.
- $60-2d=42$: $d=9$. Angles $24,33,42,51,60,69,78,87,96$, forming triangles $(24,69,87)$, $(33,51,96)$, $(42,60,78)$. Largest angle $96^\circ$.
- $60-d=42$: $d=18$, but then the smallest angle would be $60-72<0$. Impossible.

**Answer: $78^\circ$, $84^\circ$ or $96^\circ$** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2024-c5.title: Set up two equations
ukmt-cayley-2024-c5.body:
Let there be $x$ groups of $2$, $y$ groups of $6$ and $z$ groups of $10$.

*Mean group size $5$:* $2x+6y+10z=5(x+y+z)$, i.e. $y=3x-5z$. (1)

*Mean answer $7$:* the $2x$ people in pairs answer $1$, the $6y$ people in sixes answer $5$, the $10z$ people in tens answer $9$. The total of the answers is $2x+30y+90z$, and the number of people is $2x+6y+10z$, so
$$2x+30y+90z=7(2x+6y+10z)\iff 12x+12y=20z\iff 3x+3y=5z. \qquad (2)$$

Substitute $y=3x-5z$ from (1) into (2): $3x+9x-15z=5z$, so $12x=20z$, i.e. $3x=5z$. Then (1) gives $y=3x-5z=0$.

So there are no groups of $6$ people. ∎

ukmt-cayley-2024-c6.title: Reduce to one condition modulo 9
ukmt-cayley-2024-c6.body:
A number is divisible by $9$ exactly when its digit sum is. Let row $i$ ($1\le i\le9$) start with the digit $a_i\in\{1,\dots,9\}$. Then the entry in row $i$, column $j$ is congruent to $a_i+j-1 \pmod 9$.

- *Rows:* each row contains $1,\dots,9$, with digit sum $45$, a multiple of $9$. So every row is fine.
- *Column $j$:* the digit sum is $\equiv\sum_i a_i+9(j-1)\equiv \sum a_i\pmod 9$.
- *Diagonal from top-left:* entries $(i,i)$ have sum $\equiv\sum a_i+(0+1+\dots+8)=\sum a_i+36\equiv\sum a_i$.
- *Diagonal from bottom-left:* entries $(i,10-i)$ have sum $\equiv\sum a_i+\sum_i(9-i)=\sum a_i+36\equiv\sum a_i$.

So the grid is gorgeous exactly when $a_1+a_2+\dots+a_9\equiv0\pmod 9$.

*Counting:* choose $a_1,\dots,a_8$ freely ($9^8$ ways). Then exactly one value $a_9\in\{1,\dots,9\}$ makes the total a multiple of $9$ (one value in each residue class). So there are $9^8=43\,046\,721$ gorgeous grids.

**Answer: $9^8=43\,046\,721$** ∎
